page: Amazon Web Services t8i.medium is a burstable, entry-level general-purpose instance powered by the AWS Nitro System. It is configured with an Intel Xeon 6975P-C processor clocked at 3.9 GHz, featuring 1 physical core and 2 vCPUs via hyperthreading on the x86_64 architecture. The underlying CPU supports advanced instruction sets, including AVX-512 variants, AMX (tile and int8), and hardware-accelerated cryptography via AES, VAES, and SHA-NI. The host platform integrates 480 MB of L3 cache, with 48 KB of L1d and 2 MB of L2 cache available per core structure. Memory consists of 4.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 operating at 7 GHz (2.0 GB per core). This instance includes no dedicated local storage, no GPUs, and has a 0 Gbps baseline network bandwidth profile.

Benchmark results highlight strong single-core execution alongside typical limitations of a low-core burstable allocation. In single-threaded workloads, the instance achieves top-quartile results with a Geekbench single-core score of 2,186.0, single-threaded gzip compression at 34.24 GB/sec, and bzip3 decompression at 14.47 GB/sec. Stress-ng single-core tests place it in the average tier at 2,109.58. In contrast, multi-threaded metrics reflect the single physical core constraint, yielding bottom-tier figures such as a multi-core stress-ng score of 2,151.29 and a Geekbench multi-core score of 2,807.0. Memory bandwidth remains lower-tier, recording 27.29 GB/sec read and 17.28 GB/sec write for uncached 256 MB blocks, although static web serving achieves average throughput at 7.27 GB/sec.

Cost efficiency is centered on workloads that require brief CPU bursts and low continuous utilization rather than sustained high-throughput execution. The burstable CPU model makes it economical for intermittent processing without paying for continuous multi-core capacity, though prolonged CPU-heavy tasks will encounter throttling tradeoffs. The absence of local disk requires external volume attachments for persistent storage.

The t8i.medium is suited for small-scale web servers, lightweight microservices, build steps with minimal thread requirements, background utility tasks, and development environments requiring recent instruction set extensions like AMX and AVX-512.
